chapter.title: Tools: what the intern is allowed to touch

cards.body: Picture the intern's first morning. You hand them a laminated card: *may use: the company search engine, the shared drive (read only), the printer.* **Everything the intern can do to the world is on that card.** They can think all they like, but if 'send email' is not printed on it, no email leaves the building.
cards.simpler: Imagine a new intern's first morning. You hand them a small card that says what they may use: the company search engine, the shared drive for reading only, and the printer. **Everything the intern can do to the world is on that card.** They can think as much as they like. But if 'send email' is not on the card, no email goes out. The card is the whole limit.

cards.prompt: The intern's card has 3 lines: search the web, read a file, add a calendar event. Halfway through a task they decide the best next step is to delete a file. What happens?

options.text: The file gets deleted. A clever intern finds a way.
Nothing. Delete is not on the card, so the request has nowhere to go.
They ask the search engine to delete it instead.

whyNot.a: That's imagining the intern has hands of their own. The model only writes requests; code performs them, and there is no delete code to perform this one.
whyNot.c: That's mixing up two tools. Search can only search; a tool does the one job its name says.

cards.reteach: The model never touches anything directly. It writes a request like 'use tool: delete_file'. If no such tool is on the list, the request is just text that goes nowhere.

cards.title: The card, and the request
cards.body:
A *tool* is a named action the agent may ask for, with a short description: 'search_web: takes a phrase, returns the top 5 results.' The model reads this list at the start, like reading the laminated card.

When the model decides to act, it does not act. It writes a small structured request: *tool: search_web, query: cheapest flight Lisbon March*. **The model only writes the request; ordinary code performs it** and hands the result back as plain text.

So the model's whole power over the world is borrowed. It can wish for anything, but it gets only what the code is willing to do.
cards.simpler: A tool is a named action the agent is allowed to ask for. It comes with a short note, like 'search_web: give it a phrase, get the top 5 results.' The model reads this list at the start, like reading the card. When the model wants to act, it does not act. It writes a short request: 'tool: search_web, query: cheapest flight Lisbon March.' **The model only writes the request; ordinary code performs it** and hands back the result as plain text. So the model's power is borrowed. It can wish for anything, but it only gets what the code will do.

cards.title: Priya's news agent
cards.body: Priya builds a tiny agent to find and summarise 3 recent news stories about electric bikes. She gives it 2 tools: search_web and fetch_page. The log shows the model asking search_web for 'electric bike news', then fetch_page 3 times, then writing the summary with no tool at all. At one point the model writes 'I will now email this to Priya.' **Nothing happens.** There is no email tool, so the sentence is just a sentence.
cards.simpler: Priya builds a small agent to find and sum up 3 recent news stories about electric bikes. She gives it 2 tools: search_web and fetch_page. The log shows the model asking search_web for 'electric bike news', then using fetch_page 3 times, then writing the summary with no tool at all. At one point the model writes 'I will now email this to Priya.' **Nothing happens.** There is no email tool, so that sentence is just a sentence.

cards.prompt: Priya now wants the summary saved as a note on her laptop. Which change actually gets her there?

options.text: Write the goal more firmly: 'You MUST save the file.'
Add a write_file tool, with code behind it that really writes to disk.
Describe her laptop in detail so the model understands where notes live.

whyNot.a: That's changing the goal, not the card. A firmer wish is still only text, with no code to carry it out.
whyNot.c: That's more knowledge, not more reach. Knowing where notes live gives the model no way to put one there.

cards.reteach: An agent gains a new ability only when a new tool is added: a name the model can ask for, plus code that does the job. More words in the prompt never add abilities.

cards.title: The list is the lever
cards.body:
Flip it round. Because every action goes through the list, **the tool list is the single biggest safety lever you have.** Shorten it and the worst the agent can do shrinks with it.

Tools are not equally risky. Reading things (search, open a file) is cheap to get wrong: a bad read gives a bad answer, and you can ignore it. Changing things (send, delete, pay, post) is where mistakes become real. An email sent to the wrong person cannot be unsent.

So before handing over a tool, ask: if the model calls this at the worst moment with the worst input, what breaks? That answer decides whether it goes on the card.
cards.simpler: Turn it around. Every action goes through the list, so **the tool list is the single biggest safety lever you have.** Make it shorter and the worst the agent can do gets smaller too. Tools are not all equally risky. Reading things, like search or open a file, is cheap to get wrong. A bad read gives a bad answer, and you can ignore it. Changing things, like send, delete, pay or post, is where mistakes become real. A wrong email cannot be unsent. So before you hand over a tool, ask: if the model calls this at the worst moment with the worst input, what breaks? That answer decides if it goes on the card.

cards.body: Tomas wanted his agent to tidy his inbox, so he gave it one big tool called 'gmail' that could read, archive, reply and delete. It read fine. Then it tidied 3 unread invoices into the bin. **Spot it by looking for a tool named after a whole app rather than one verb**: that tool is hiding a delete inside a read.
cards.simpler: Tomas wanted his agent to tidy his inbox. He gave it one big tool called 'gmail' that could read, archive, reply and delete. Reading went fine. Then it tidied 3 unread invoices into the bin. **Spot it by looking for a tool named after a whole app rather than one verb.** A tool like that is hiding a delete inside a read, the way one master key opens every door.

cards.prompt: A friend says: 'My agent can only search and read files, so it can't do much harm. But I'm worried it might book a hotel by accident.' What do you tell them?

options.text: It can't. Booking is not a tool it has, so no request for it goes anywhere.
It might, if the model is smart enough to work out booking on its own.
It might, because reading a file about hotels teaches it how.

whyNot.b: That's confusing cleverness with reach. The model's smarts change what it asks for, never what code exists to answer.
whyNot.c: That's mixing knowledge with ability. A read tool returns text; reading how to book gives it no booking tool.

cards.reteach: The model's reach is exactly the tool list, nothing more. Search and read can produce bad answers, but they cannot change anything in the world.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: An agent acts only by asking for named tools that ordinary code then performs, so **the model never touches anything itself.** Keep the list short, and be slowest to hand over anything that changes the world rather than reads it.
cards.simpler: An agent acts only by asking for named tools, and ordinary code then performs them. So **the model never touches anything itself.** Keep the list short. Be slowest to hand over any tool that changes the world, and quicker with one that only reads it. A reading mistake gives a bad answer. A changing mistake, like a sent email, cannot be taken back.

cards.body: Pick one chore you would hand an agent tonight. Write the tools it would need as single verbs: search, read, send. Circle the one that changes something. That is the one to watch.
cards.simpler: Pick one chore you would hand an agent tonight. Write down the tools it would need as single verbs: search, read, send. Then circle the one that changes something instead of just reading it. That is the one to watch. It is the tool that can do real harm if it runs at the wrong moment with the wrong input.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now list the tools an agent needs for a task and point to the one that changes the world, so needs the most care.
